title: Official Help and Alerts
intro: Official warnings and instructions reach you through several channels, and each of them fails sometimes. This module makes sure you can receive them, know which offices are behind them, and know how to join in if you want to help.
credit: Based on Unit 8 of Oregon's Be 2 Weeks Ready toolkit

actions.title: Find the radio and TV stations that carry emergency broadcasts for your area
actions.why: When phones and the internet are down, broadcast radio is the channel most likely to still carry official instructions.
actions.how: Look on your city or county emergency management website for the stations that carry Emergency Alert System messages locally; they are often listed under 'alerts' or 'stay informed'. If none are listed, use your main local news stations on AM and FM and the nearest public radio station. Write down three, each with its name and frequency. You do not sign up for these broadcasts; you only need to know where to tune.
actions.done: Three local stations are written down on paper, each with its name and frequency.

actions.title: Write the station numbers on your emergency radio and save them as presets
actions.why: In a power cut you will not be able to look up a frequency, so it has to be on the radio already.
actions.how: Write the three frequencies on a strip of tape and stick it to your battery or hand-crank radio. Tune the radio to the first one and leave it there. If you have a car, save the same stations as presets on its radio.
actions.done: A strip of tape on your radio shows the three frequencies, the radio is tuned to the first, and any car radio has the same stations saved as presets.
actions.apartment: Without a car, the battery radio at home is your only broadcast receiver, so also copy the frequencies onto the back of your wallet contact card (CM-02).

actions.title: Find your NOAA Weather Radio frequency
actions.why: The weather band carries official forecasts and warnings around the clock and needs no phone signal or internet.
actions.how: In the United States, NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts from the nearest National Weather Service office on one of seven frequencies between 162.400 and 162.550 MHz. Go to weather.gov/nwr, find the transmitter for your county and write its frequency on the tape on your radio. Switch the radio to its weather band and check that you can hear the broadcast from the room where you would shelter. Outside the United States, find your national weather service's warning channel instead.
actions.done: Your county's weather band frequency is written on the tape on your radio, and you have heard the broadcast from the room where you would shelter.
actions.apartment: Concrete and steel weaken radio signals, so in an apartment test reception beside a window on each side of your home and note which one works.

actions.title: Learn what your area's outdoor sirens sound like and what they mean
actions.why: A siren helps only if you recognize it and already know what it is telling you to do.
actions.how: Check your city or county emergency management website for whether your area has outdoor warning sirens, what they warn of (tornado, tsunami, a dam, a chemical plant) and when they are tested; many are tested on a fixed day each month. Listen to the next test so that you know the sound. Write down what the siren means where you live and the action that goes with it, such as 'go indoors and tune in' or, on a tsunami coast, 'go to high ground'.
actions.done: Whether your area has sirens, what they mean and the action that goes with them are written down, and you have listened to one test if there are any.
actions.apartment: Sirens are meant to be heard outdoors and may not carry through closed windows on an upper floor, so do not count on hearing one at home; keep phone alerts switched on (U2-10).

actions.title: Learn what a ShakeAlert earthquake warning is and what to do when one arrives
actions.why: An earthquake warning gives you seconds, not minutes, so your response has to be decided beforehand.
actions.how: ShakeAlert is the earthquake early-warning system for the US West Coast. It detects an earthquake that has already begun and sends a warning to phones in the area through Wireless Emergency Alerts and apps; it does not predict earthquakes. You do not register for it: keep emergency alerts switched on (U2-10). When a warning arrives, do not stop to look for more information: drop, cover and hold on at once (U2-161).
actions.done: Every phone in the home shows emergency alerts switched on, and everyone at home has heard the rule: when a warning arrives, drop, cover and hold on at once.

region.label: Earthquake country
region.general: Elsewhere, learn the sound and meaning of the warnings used where you live: tornado or tsunami sirens, and the alert tones on your phone.

actions.apartment: On an upper floor the swaying is stronger and lasts longer: get down beside an inside wall away from windows, stay there until it stops, then use the stairs, not the elevator (HR-18).
actions.cite_todo: An official page naming the states ShakeAlert covers and confirming delivery through Wireless Emergency Alerts; the USGS page confirms only that it detects earthquakes already under way and reaches phones in several ways.

actions.section: Know the people and offices near you
actions.title: Talk with neighbors and coworkers about plans, skills and who may need help
actions.why: The first help after any emergency comes from the people already beside you, and it works better when you know each other.
actions.how: Start one conversation this week with a neighbor and one with a coworker. Ask three things: do you have a plan for a long power outage; is there something you are good at that would help, such as first aid, languages or repairs; and would you or anyone you know need a hand, for example with stairs, carrying water or collecting medicines? Offer your own answers too. Keep what you learn to yourself and pass on only what people have agreed to share.
actions.done: One neighbor and one coworker have each answered your three questions and heard your own answers.
actions.apartment: In an apartment building start with the doors on your own floor and swap phone numbers (NB-01); those are the people who can reach you when the elevators are out.

actions.section: Know the people and offices near you
actions.title: Bookmark your local and state emergency management websites
actions.why: These offices issue evacuation orders, open shelters and post verified updates, so you want to know where to find them before you need them.
actions.how: Search for the name of your city or county plus 'emergency management', then your state or province plus 'emergency management'. Check that each address is an official government one, such as a .gov domain. On each site find three things: the hazards they plan for in your area, how they send alerts, and where they post updates during an incident. Bookmark both sites on every phone in the household.
actions.done: Your city or county emergency management website and your state's are bookmarked on every phone in the household.

actions.section: Know the people and offices near you
actions.title: Follow your city and county emergency offices on social media
actions.why: During an incident these accounts often carry the newest official updates between formal alerts.
actions.how: On the platforms you already use, follow the official accounts of your city and county emergency management offices and your fire department. Reach the accounts through the links on the offices' own websites, so that you do not follow an imitation. Turn on notifications for these accounts only. Treat social media as an extra: it needs data and battery, so it does not replace phone alerts and a radio.
actions.done: The platforms you use show you following your city and county emergency offices and your fire department, with notifications on for those accounts only.

actions.section: Know the people and offices near you
actions.title: Check before you share
actions.why: Rumors spread fastest when networks are patchy, and a false report about water, shelters or evacuation can send people the wrong way.
actions.how: Before you pass on anything during an emergency, check it against an official source: your emergency management office's website or account, the utility, or the radio stations on your list. If you cannot confirm it, do not forward it. When you share official information, include where it came from and the time it was issued, because instructions change. Be wary of screenshots, forwarded voice notes and any message that asks for money or personal details.
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard the rule: check it against an official source first, and do not forward what you cannot confirm.

actions.section: Know the people and offices near you
actions.title: Ask your local emergency agency what resources and volunteer roles it has
actions.why: Local emergency offices often have free guides, classes and volunteer roles that residents never hear about unless they ask.
actions.how: Phone or email the office using the contact on its website, or post a question to its official account. Ask three things: what free materials, classes or events it offers residents; whether it has advice specific to your neighborhood or type of building; and what volunteer roles exist and what training they need. Write down the answers and the name of the person you spoke to.
actions.done: The office's answers to your three questions are written down with the name of the person you spoke to.
actions.apartment: Ask specifically whether the office has guidance or a speaker for apartment and condominium buildings; your management or residents' association may be glad to host one (NB-06).

actions.section: Know the people and offices near you
actions.title: Save your utilities' outage maps and report lines, and your city's non-emergency number
actions.why: In an outage you need to report the fault, see the estimated repair time and keep 911 free for emergencies.
actions.how: For each utility that serves your home (electricity, gas, water), find the outage map page and the phone number for reporting an outage or a leak; both are on the bill and the utility's website. Bookmark the maps and save the numbers in every phone, along with your city's non-emergency number (311 in many North American cities) and your building's after-hours number. Then write them all by hand on the printable utilities list, because a dead phone holds no numbers. If you smell gas or hear hissing, get everyone out at once. Touch no switches, appliances or phones on the way, and do not stop to find or turn a valve. Do not go back in. From a safe distance call the gas utility's emergency number or 911. Only the utility turns the gas back on.
actions.done: Each utility's outage map is bookmarked, and its report number, your city's non-emergency number and your building's after-hours number are in every phone and on your Utilities list.
actions.apartment: If your building pays the utility bills, ask management which companies supply it and whether you or they report an outage, and note the answer with the building's after-hours number (HR-01).

actions.section: Keep your alerts up to date
actions.title: Check that your local alert registration is current
actions.why: An alert system can reach only the phone number, email and address it has on file.
actions.how: If you have not yet signed up for your city or county alert system, do that first (U2-09). If you have, sign in and check four things: your cell number, your email, your home address including the unit number, and which alert types and languages are switched on. Check again whenever you move or change your number or email. Add "update emergency alerts" to your moving checklist and to your yearly review, and check every adult's entry, not just your own. If you have moved to a new area, sign up again with that area's system.
actions.done: Your alert account shows your current cell number, email and home address with unit number, and the alert types and languages you want switched on.

actions.section: Keep your alerts up to date
actions.title: Add the other addresses you want alerts for
actions.why: Your household is spread across the city for most of the day, and a warning for a school or workplace matters as much as one for home.
actions.how: Most local alert systems let one account hold several addresses. Add each place a household member spends the day, such as workplaces, schools and childcare (use your notes from X1-05), and the home of any relative you look out for. If a place is in another city or county, sign up with that area's system as well. Offer to register a relative's own phone too, since some systems call landlines. In the FEMA app you can follow up to five locations anywhere in the United States.
actions.done: Your alert account lists each workplace, school and childcare address your household uses and the home of any relative you look out for.

actions.section: Keep your alerts up to date
actions.title: Sign up for transit alerts
actions.why: If you rely on buses or trains, a suspended service changes how you get home or get out, and you want to know before you reach the stop.
actions.how: Find your transit agency's alerts page or app and subscribe by text or email to the lines you use most: the routes between home, work and school, plus one alternative for each. Do the same for any regional rail or ferry service you use, and save the agency's information phone line. Drivers gain from this too, because transit shutdowns and road closures are often announced together.
actions.done: Your phone or email shows you subscribed to alerts for the lines you use most, and the agency's information line is saved in your phone.

actions.title: Offer your help to your local emergency management office
actions.why: Emergency management offices are small, and residents who are already prepared are the help they can call on.
actions.how: Contact the office and say that you and your neighbors are working through a two-week readiness program and would like to help. Ask what they most need from residents, which volunteer teams they run or know of, and when the next introduction session is. Choose one thing you can commit to, even if it is only passing their preparedness material to your neighbors.
actions.done: The office has replied saying what it needs from residents, and you have told them the one thing you will do.
actions.apartment: Offer your building as a way to reach many households at once, with a table in the lobby or a talk in the common room.

actions.title: Take Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) training
actions.why: Trained residents can look after their own household and neighbors safely while professional responders are stretched.
actions.how: CERT is a FEMA-backed course, usually free, run locally by fire departments and emergency management offices. It teaches residents basic disaster skills: fire safety, light search and rescue, disaster first aid and working as a team. Search for your city or county plus 'CERT', or ask your emergency management office for the next course. Ask whether it is offered in other languages or adapted for access needs if that would help you.
actions.done: Your place on the next local course is confirmed in writing by the organizer, or you have already finished one.
actions.apartment: A building with two or three CERT-trained residents has the start of a floor-warden team (NB-06, NB-11).
